lead.t: Acute bacterial meningitis: Life-threatening acute purulent infection of the leptomeninges (pia mater, arachnoid mater) and the subarachnoid space, characterized by meningism and neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis.

b: $\rightarrow$ Secretion of IgA proteases enables mucosal attachment and invasion
$\rightarrow$ Intravascular survival via antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule
$\rightarrow$ Crossing of the blood-brain barrier via cerebral capillaries or choroid plexus
$\rightarrow$ Rapid bacterial replication in the subarachnoid space (low baseline complement/antibodies)

snip.t: Depressed GCS, focal deficits, or seizures signal cerebral malaria, bacterial meningitis, or intracranial tuberculoma/toxoplasmosis.
| Acute bacterial meningitis | Fever, severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness | Lumbar puncture: cloudy CSF, neutrophilia |
Bacterial Meningitis: Both cause headache, fever, and neck stiffness.
Look-alike conditions: Typhoid fever, bacterial meningitis, severe anaemia from other causes, viral hepatitis.

*By the end of this note, the student will be able to distinguish, investigate, and clinically manage bacterial meningitis and encephalitis in a Kenyan ward setting; verify all drug choices and regimens against the Kenya MoH guidelines and local hospital formularies.*
Infectious: HIV (neuro‑candidiasis, CMV, HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder), cerebral malaria, tuberculous meningitis, bacterial meningitis, neuro‑borreliosis (rare).

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT the most important cause of acute bacterial meningitis?
qs.e: *S. pyogenes* is not a major cause of bacterial meningitis; the other three (pneumococcus, meningococcus, *H. influenzae*) are classic major causes depending on age group.

qs.q: Which cephalosporin has the best CNS penetration and is used for bacterial meningitis?
o: and has a long half-life allowing once or twice-daily dosing.
qs.e: Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin with excellent CSF penetration, especially in inflamed meninges. It's effective against common meningitis pathogens (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae) and has a long half-life allowing once or twice-daily dosing.

qs.q: The most common cause of acute bacterial meningitis in adults is
qs.e: S. pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults and elderly, accounting for approximately 50% of cases. It also causes pneumonia, otitis media, and sinusitis.

qs.q: Which organism is NOT among the major common causes of acute bacterial meningitis?
qs.e: Streptococcus pyogenes is an uncommon cause of acute bacterial meningitis. Common causes vary with age and setting but include S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis, with S. agalactiae important in neonates.

qs.q: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults.
qs.e: While Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b are significant causes of bacterial meningitis, Streptococcus pneumoniae is considered the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults in many parts of the world, particularly in developed countries.

qs.q: The most common cause of acute bacterial meningitis in adults is Streptococcus pneumoniae.
qs.e: In adults, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis. While Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae are also significant pathogens, S. pneumoniae is generally considered the most common in this age group.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a most important cause of acute bacterial meningitis?
qs.e: While E. coli can cause meningitis, particularly in neonates, it is not considered one of the most important causes of acute bacterial meningitis in the general adult population, which is dominated by S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis, with H. influenzae type b being a significant cause in unvaccinated children.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Microbiology Exam - June 5, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a most important cause of acute bacterial meningitis in adults?
qs.e: While Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) is a significant cause of bacterial meningitis, its incidence in adults has drastically decreased due to vaccination. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the most common causes in adults.

ai.title: Bacterial Meningitis
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A life‑threatening infection of the leptomeninges presenting with fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered consciousness. Rapid diagnosis and empiric antibiotics are essential, especially in low‑resource settings where delays can be fatal.

sections.p: Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection of the pia and arachnoid mater. It is caused by encapsulated organisms that colonise the nasopharynx and breach the blood‑brain barrier. In East Africa, the most common pathogens are *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Neisseria meningitidis* and *Haemophilus influenzae* type b.
b: High mortality if untreated; early empiric therapy saves lives
Clinical triad: fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status

sections.p: The key virulence factor is the polysaccharide capsule, which prevents phagocytosis and complement activation. IgA proteases aid mucosal attachment, and the bacteria can survive in blood and cross the cerebral capillaries or choroid plexus.
Transmission is via respiratory droplets. Colonisation of the nasopharynx is common; invasive disease occurs when the capsule breaches mucosal barriers and enters the bloodstream.

The infection spreads to the subarachnoid space, causing neutrophilic pleocytosis, increased intracranial pressure and potential cerebral infarction. In low‑resource settings, co‑infections (HIV, malaria, TB) worsen outcomes.
b: Risk of seizures and focal deficits

sections.p: Clinical suspicion is followed by a lumbar puncture if safe. CSF should be analysed for cell count, protein, glucose and Gram stain. In settings without LP, a rapid antigen test or bedside ultrasound may be used.

t.b: Is CSF neutrophilic and protein‑rich? A neutrophilic pleocytosis with high protein and low glucose confirms bacterial meningitis.
Shows Gram‑positive cocci in chains (pneumococcus) or Gram‑negative diplococci (meningococcus). Positive stain directs empiric therapy.
Detects *N. meningitidis* or *H. influenzae* in CSF; a positive result supports empiric coverage.
Rule out mass lesions or increased ICP before LP; a normal scan allows safe LP.

sections.p: Empiric therapy must cover the most likely organisms and be started immediately after a safe LP or, if unavailable, before LP. Supportive care includes fluid management, seizure control and monitoring for complications.

t.b: Treats *S. pneumoniae* and *N. meningitidis*. It penetrates CSF well and is bactericidal.
Coverage for Listeria in patients >50 or immunocompromised; not needed in most East African adults.
Added if local resistance patterns suggest high MIC for ceftriaxone; monitor renal function.
Alternative when ceftriaxone is unavailable; avoid in patients with G6PD deficiency.

sections.p: Remember the triad but also look for altered consciousness, seizures or focal deficits, which raise the suspicion of complications. In low‑resource settings, a normal CSF glucose can be misleading if the patient is hypoglycaemic. Always consider HIV and malaria co‑infection.
b: Altered GCS, seizures, focal signs → higher mortality

sections.p: Viral meningitis, cerebral malaria, tuberculous meningitis and meningococcal sepsis can mimic bacterial meningitis.
b: Viral meningitis: lymphocytic CSF, milder course

sections.p: CSF glucose may be normal in early disease; a negative Gram stain does not exclude bacteria. In malaria, fever and headache may mask meningitis.
b: Negative Gram stain → still treat empirically

sections.p: Treat the cause, then supportive care and monitoring. Avoid drugs that increase intracranial pressure or cause haemorrhage.
Any patient with fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness requires urgent assessment. In low‑resource settings, do not delay LP if the patient is unstable.

t.a: What is the first step if a lumbar puncture cannot be performed?
t.b: Start empiric antibiotics immediately after a safe clinical assessment and consider a CT scan if contraindications exist.

t.a: Why is ceftriaxone chosen as first‑line?
t.b: It has excellent CSF penetration, a broad spectrum against the most common pathogens and a favourable safety profile.
Cerebral malaria can present with seizures and altered consciousness but CSF is usually normal; it must be ruled out in endemic areas.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever with neck stiffness and altered consciousness
Rapid deterioration or high ICP signs

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with fever, stiff neck and seizures. What is the next step? — Perform a CT scan if contraindications to LP; start empiric ceftriaxone and ampicillin immediately.
An adult with suspected meningitis has a normal CSF glucose. What does this suggest? — Early disease or possible malaria; still treat empirically.
Why is ampicillin added to ceftriaxone in patients over 50? — To cover Listeria monocytogenes, which is more common in the elderly.
A patient with HIV presents with fever and neck stiffness. Which organism is most likely? — Streptococcus pneumoniae; HIV increases risk of bacterial meningitis.
What complication is most feared in bacterial meningitis? — Cerebral infarction due to vasculitis; monitor for focal deficits.
When is dexamethasone indicated in bacterial meningitis? — In children with pneumococcal meningitis to reduce hearing loss.
